notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Luke 9:22–41. Some pages were cut off when I opened them: the Enduring Word chapter page, the Pulpit Commentary chapter page and a Blue Letter Bible copy of Guzik. Because of that, some verses have only a little material, and v. 36 has nothing. I found no Catholic, Orthodox, Wesleyan or Pentecostal-site sources, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on these verses, so those headings are left out.

---

**v. 22**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "Elders, chief priests, and scribes" is simply a popular way of describing the great council of the Jewish nation, the Sanhedrin, made up of those three groups. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/9.htm
- **Henry's Complete Commentary**, quoted on StudyLight, has a related point. Jesus told the disciples to keep quiet about His being the Messiah because, "the whole Jewish concept of the Messiah was the establishing of the kingdom and the overthrow of the kingdoms of the world. And they did not understand that He was to come into the kingdom by His death." — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-27.html

**v. 23**
- **Who is "all"?** Gill reads it as not only to all the disciples, but "to the multitude", following Mark 8:34. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/9-23.htm. Constable instead says the "all" must be the disciples in view of the context (Luke 9:18). — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-23.html
- **The cross image (Guzik):** In Roman times a condemned man carried his own cross, or its crossbeam, to execution. No one "took up" a real cross willingly, yet Jesus says His followers must take theirs up voluntarily. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
- **"Daily" (Guzik):** Guzik treats "deny himself" and "take up his cross" as the same idea. He says the word "daily" shows Jesus is speaking spiritually, since no one could be crucified literally everyday. Daily they could have the same attitude as Jesus had. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
- **"Daily" in other commentators:**
  - Ellicott notes the word is found only in Luke and compares Paul's "I die daily" (1 Cor 15:31). — https://biblehub.com/luke/9-23.htm
  - The Geneva notes say one cross follows another just as one day follows another. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/9-23.htm
  - Clarke points out that "daily" is missing from many reputable manuscripts and from the parallels in Matthew and Mark. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-23.html
- **Choosing crosses (Matthew Henry):** We must not bring crosses on ourselves, yet, when they are laid for us, we must take them up, and carry them after Christ. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/9-23.htm
- **Greek tenses (bible.org, Utley):** "Deny" and "take up" are one-time commands, while "follow" is ongoing. In his words, "There is a gate and then a road (cf. Matt. 7:13-14). There is an initial response and an ongoing response." — https://bible.org/book/export/html/21306
- **Where traditions differ – is this verse about how to be saved, or how to live as a disciple?**
  - **Baptist (John MacArthur):** He calls this a gospel invitation, in which Jesus sets the terms for sinners: Self denial, cross bearing daily, and loyal obedient following. — https://www.gty.org/sermons/42-122/the-gospel-in-perspective
  - **Restoration Movement (Coffman):** Similarly, he says This is the plan of salvation. For him, denying oneself means claiming nothing of one's own as the basis for being saved. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-23.html
  - **Dispensational (Constable):** He reads it as a disciple's particular burden: Jesus meant that His disciples had to bear a particular burden that non-disciples did not have to bear. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-23.html
  - **Methodist (Benson):** He applies "daily" strictly: that day is lost wherein no cross is taken up. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/9-23.htm
- **Note against a common misreading (Precept Austin):** Taking up the cross is not just putting up with an unavoidable trial such as illness. It is something to be actively chosen each day. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-9-commentary
- **Note against prosperity readings (Precept Austin):** The page says Jesus did not offer His disciples a life of prosperity and ease but called them to self-sacrifice and identification with Him. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-9-commentary

**vv. 24–25**
- **MacArthur:** He sums up the paradox this way: You win by losing. You live by dying. — https://www.gty.org/sermons/42-119/the-starting-principle-of-discipleship
- **Matthew Henry on v. 25:** Matthew and Mark say "lose his own soul" where Luke says "lose himself", which plainly intimates that our souls are ourselves. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-23.html

**v. 26**
- **Gill:** This coming in glory points to the last day, when the Son of Man will show His displeasure at all who were ashamed of Him. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/9-27.htm

**v. 27** (the most debated verse in this passage)
- **The transfiguration view:**
  - GotQuestions takes this as the most natural reading, because the transfiguration comes next in all three Gospels. — https://www.gotquestions.org/not-taste-death.html
  - Constable agrees and sees the transfiguration as a preview of the kingdom (cf. 2 Pet 1:16–18). — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-27.html
  - A Bible Hub article says Irenaeus and Origen took it chiefly this way. — https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_some_will_not_taste_death.htm
- **The resurrection or Pentecost view:**
  - The Pulpit Commentary rejects both the transfiguration and the fall of Jerusalem as inadequate. It sees fulfilment in the disciples who were changed by the risen Christ during the forty days after Easter. — https://biblehub.com/luke/9-27.htm
  - Coffman sees a prophecy of the founding of the kingdom at the first Pentecost after the resurrection. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-27.html
  - The Expositor's Greek Testament says Luke probably understood it as the beginning of the church at Pentecost. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/9-27.htm
- **A combined view (Gill and Henry):** The gospel age taking hold after the resurrection and the outpouring of the Spirit, together with the destruction of the Jewish nation. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-27.html
- **Where traditions differ on the kingdom:**
  - **Reformed (Ligonier):** The saying refers to Jesus receiving the kingdom from the Father in fulfilment of Daniel 7. That is the *start* of the kingdom, as distinct from its completion at the Second Coming. — https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/some-standing-here-will-not-taste-death-unfolding-biblical-eschatology
  - **Dispensational (Constable):** He holds that Jesus foresaw the consequent postponement of the messianic kingdom. He argues that the other views have to redefine the kingdom away from the Old Testament picture of an earthly reign. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-27.html
  - **Brethren (Kelly):** In a similar way, he says the system of glory is only postponed, and in no wise given up. — same URL.
- **Modern sceptical claim and a reply (Barclay):** Barclay notes that some say Jesus wrongly expected to return within His hearers' lifetime. He denies this, reading it as a promise that they would see signs of the kingdom on its way. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-27.html

**v. 28**
- **"About eight days":** Matthew's "six" and Luke's "about eight" are explained as inclusive counting. — https://biblehub.com/luke/9-27.htm
- **Purpose of the event (Pulpit):** It was mainly meant to raise the fainting spirits of his own, to inspire them with greater confidence in himself after Jesus had spoken of suffering. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/9.htm
- **Prayer (Henry):** Christ was transfigured while praying: When Christ humbled himself to pray, he was thus exalted. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-31.html

**v. 29**
- **Henry on Luke's wording:** Luke does not use the word "transfigured", perhaps because it had been used so much in the Pagan theology, and uses an equivalent phrase instead. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-31.html
- **Pulpit:** The garments were literally "lightening forth", as if lit from some glorious light inside. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/9.htm
- **Guzik:** For a short time Jesus looked more like the King of Glory than a humble man. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Luk/Luk_9.cfm

**v. 30**
- **What Moses and Elijah stand for:** A common view is that they represent the Law and the Prophets. Both also left this life in unusual ways (Deut 34; 2 Kings 2). — https://biblehub.com/luke/9-30.htm
- **Constable:** Luke calls them simply "men", which suggests Jesus is greater than both. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-30.html

**v. 31**
- **"Departure":** The Greek word is *exodos*, recalling Israel's escape from Egypt. Only Luke tells us what they talked about.
  - Constable says Jesus' death would bring redemption like the Exodus, but on a cosmic scale. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-31.html
  - Bengel says the word covers the passion, cross, death, resurrection and ascension. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/9-31.htm
  - Gill, following Lightfoot, includes the ascension. — same URL.
  - Vincent's Word Studies notes that Moses and Joshua began an exodus, but did not "accomplish" the final going out of God's people. — same URL.

**v. 32**
- **The sleep (Barnes):** This may have been at night, after a tiring day. The disciples fell asleep during Jesus' prayer, not while the transfiguration itself was happening. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-30.html

**v. 33**
- **Peter's offer (Guzik):** Peter's suggestion amounted to avoiding the cross, both Jesus' cross and his own. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/
- **Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary:** those know not what they say, that talk of making tabernacles on earth for glorified saints in heaven. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/9-31.htm

**v. 34**
- **The cloud:** A Bible Hub article links the shining cloud to Sinai and Horeb, where God revealed Himself in the past. — https://biblehub.com/q/Why_do_Moses_Elijah_join_Jesus_in_Luke_9_31.htm

**v. 35**
- **"Chosen" (Pulpit):** Luke's wording differs from the "beloved Son" of Matthew and Mark. Pulpit takes this as a sign that the three accounts are separate, independent memories. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/9.htm
- **"Listen to Him":** The same Bible Hub article says this command reorders the purpose of life around obeying the Son. — https://biblehub.com/q/Why_do_Moses_Elijah_join_Jesus_in_Luke_9_31.htm

**v. 37**
- **Timing (Pulpit):** The transfiguration took place in the late evening or at night, which explains "the next day". — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/9.htm

**vv. 38–39**
- **Matthew Henry:** He stresses how cruel the spirit was and how much harm Satan does where he takes hold, But happy they that have access to Christ! — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-41.html

**v. 40**
- **Why the disciples failed:**
  - Jesus had given them authority over demons in 9:1, which makes this failure striking. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-9
  - Guzik suggests this may have been a stronger or more stubborn case of possession. He quotes Clarke: they were confused by their lack of success, but not by their lack of faith. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/luke/luke-9.cfm
  - Henry offers three possibilities: they distrusted the power, or doubted their commission, or did not pray as they should. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-41.html

**v. 41**
- **Who is Jesus rebuking?** Commentators disagree:
  - **Gill:** Not the disciples. He says the words were spoken to the father, the crowd and especially the scribes. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/9-41.htm
  - **Clarke (as cited by Henry):** The words are aimed at the disciples. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-41.html
  - **Pulpit:** Addressed to the whole crowd. — https://biblehub.com/luke/9-41.htm
  - **Utley (bible.org):** Both the disciples and the crowd. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-9
- **Old Testament echo:** Utley calls the phrase an allusion to Moses' song in Deuteronomy 32:5, 20. — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-9
- **The contrast with the mountain:** The Cambridge notes on Bible Hub link Jesus' sorrow to the contrast between the glory He had just left and the weak faith and wrangling below. They add that He could not go to His Father until He had led His disciples to faith. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/9-41.htm
- **"Bring your son here":** Despite His disappointment, Jesus moves straight to compassionate action. — https://biblehub.com/luke/9-41.htm
